title: Coinbase & Airbnb
summary: Problems whose patterns are commonly reported in Coinbase and Airbnb coding interviews, from Easy to Hard. Approximate and hand curated, not an official or verified question list.
lesson:
About this list
- Each problem practices a pattern that candidates commonly describe from Coinbase and Airbnb technical interviews: lazy iterators, transactional key-value stores, limit order books, currency conversion graphs, in-memory filesystems, interval/range modules, routing, and multi-part stateful APIs.
- Problems are grouped Easy, Medium, and Hard so you can warm up on crisp parsing and range formatting before building multi-part stateful engines.
- The selection is approximate. Interview prompts evolve and vary by team, so treat this track as practical stateful-API and graph practice rather than a prediction of what you will be asked.

What to expect
- Candidates often report multi-part, production-flavored coding rounds (building a paginated/nested iterator, a matching engine, a file system, or a currency converter) where each milestone adds a realistic requirement.
- Precision on contracts—price-time priority, transaction rollback semantics, floating-point tolerances, empty nested structures, and clean error handling—is commonly tested.
- Follow-ups often explore how to keep operations fast as state grows (for example, O(log n) range updates or O(1) cache evictions).

How to prepare
- Design small, cohesive internal types (such as a resting order, range map entry, or transaction frame) so adding a follow-up requirement stays localized.
- Verify invariants around deletion, empty collections, and tie-breaking before moving on.
- Practice both graph search (BFS/DFS with weights and topological sort) and ordered-map / heap data structures (`TreeMap`, `PriorityQueue`, `ArrayDeque`).
